books.section: Topic 6.11 Reform in the Gilded Age
Social Criticism in the Gilded Age
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Frances E. Willard, Home Protection Manual (1879)
Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889
Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives (1890)
Settlement-house counts, National Park Service and Spartacus Educational histories

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which reform movements changed American society in the period 1865–1898.

documents.title: Willard on Home Protection
documents.source: Frances E. Willard, Home Protection Manual (1879), p. 5. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The WCTU president writing a manual for temperance women, arguing that the ballot would protect their homes.
documents.text: “Home Protection is the general name given to a movement already endorsed by the W.C.T Unions of the eight states, the object of which is to secure all women above the age of twenty-one the ballot as one means for the protection of their homes from the devastation caused by the legalized traffic in strong drink.”

documents.title: The Pendleton Act on Examinations
documents.source: Pendleton Civil Service Act, Section 2, January 16, 1883. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A federal law written after Garfield’s assassination, setting the rules for hiring by merit.
documents.text: “First, for open, competitive examinations for testing the fitness of applicants for the public service now classified or to be classified hereunder.”

documents.title: Bellamy on a World Without Buying and Selling
documents.source: Edward Bellamy, Looking Backward, 2000–1887 (1888), Chapter 9. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A popular novel imagining the year 2000, written to show readers a cooperative alternative to competition.
documents.text:
“There is neither selling nor buying nowadays; the distribution of goods is effected in another way. As to the bankers, having no money we have no use for those gentry.”

“A credit corresponding to his share of the annual product of the nation is given to every citizen on the public books at the beginning of each year, and a credit card issued him with which he procures at the public storehouses, found in every community, whatever he desires whenever he desires it.”

documents.title: Carnegie on the Administration of Wealth
documents.source: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A steel maker writing for a magazine read by the educated middle class, arguing that the rich should give during their lives.
documents.text:
“There are but three modes in which surplus wealth can be disposed of. It can be left to the families of the decedents; or it can be bequeathed for public purposes; or, finally, it can be administered during their lives by its possessors. . . .

This policy would work powerfully to induce the rich man to attend to the administration of wealth during his life, which is the end that society should always have in view, as being that by far most fruitful for the people.”

documents.title: Riis on the Tenements
documents.source: Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1890), Introduction. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A Danish immigrant and police reporter writing to show comfortable readers the slum conditions they ignored.
documents.text:
“Long ago it was said that “one half of the world does not know how the other half lives.” That was true then. It did not know because it did not care. The half that was on top cared little for the struggles, and less for the fate of those who were underneath, so long as it was able to hold them there and keep its own seat.”

“To-day three-fourths of its people live in the tenements, and the nineteenth century drift of the population to the cities is sending ever-increasing multitudes to crowd them.”

documents.title: The Omaha Platform on a Nation in Ruin
documents.source: People’s Party, Omaha Platform, July 4, 1892, Preamble. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A new third party’s founding statement, written to indict the old parties and rally farmers and workers.
documents.text: “The conditions which surround us best justify our co-operation; we meet in the midst of a nation brought to the verge of moral, political, and material ruin. Corruption dominates the ballot-box, the Legislatures, the Congress, and touches even the ermine of the bench. The people are demoralized; most of the States have been compelled to isolate the voters at the polling places to prevent universal intimidation and bribery. The newspapers are largely subsidized or muzzled, public opinion silenced, business prostrated, homes covered with mortgages, labor impoverished, and the land concentrating in the hands of capitalists.”

documents.title: Settlement Houses Multiply
documents.source: Counts from the National Park Service settlement history and the Spartacus Educational settlement history.
documents.sourcing: Counts compiled by historians, showing how fast the settlement movement spread after 1886.
documents.text:
| Year | Settlement houses in the United States |
| 1886 | 1 |
| 1891 | 6 |
| 1897 | 74 |

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent of change or challenge, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as industrialization, urbanization, and the growth of corporations and cities in the Gilded Age.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Grange, the Knights of Labor, the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887, or the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document’s author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of change, showing that the same reform both challenged and left the old order standing, or explaining why one reform succeeded while another stalled.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Between 1865 and 1898 reform movements changed American society a great deal in how Americans talked about poverty, corruption, and the duties of the rich, and they built new institutions, yet the change stayed partial because the reforms reached only some people and left the corporations and machines standing.
Context: Industrialization built giant corporations and crowded cities, while the urban share of the population rose from about a quarter in 1870 to over a third in 1890, and the old middle class of small shopkeepers gave way to salaried office workers.
Evidence: Documents 1 and 7 show women’s and settlement reform at work, the ballot as home protection and houses multiplying from 1 to 74. Documents 2 and 6 show political reform, examinations for federal jobs and a new party indicting corruption.
Evidence continued: Documents 3 and 4 show rival ideas about wealth, Bellamy’s nation sharing its product and Carnegie’s rich giving while they lived. Document 5 shows what reformers faced, tenements holding three-fourths of New Yorkers.
Beyond the documents: Jane Addams opened Hull House in Chicago in 1889, Henry George’s Progress and Poverty of 1879 sold widely, and the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 outlawed combinations in restraint of trade.
Sourcing: Willard writes as a temperance leader recruiting women, while Carnegie writes as a rich man defending his own class to magazine readers; the Omaha Platform is a party’s own case for itself, so its charges are a program, not a neutral report.
Complexity: Reform changed the argument about American life more than the life itself, since new institutions and laws grew beside tenements, trusts, and machines that reform never displaced.
